articles.title: For 39 years, Marilyn Hampton worked as a janitor at a Texas school district and spent her days brightening children’s lives, once believing she had failed because she never went to college; now an elementary school is being named after her
articles.summary: For 39 years, Marilyn Hampton worked as a custodian at a school district in Texas, US, cleaning buildings and helping children whenever she could.
articles.body: For 39 years, Marilyn Hampton worked as a custodian at a school district in Texas, US, cleaning buildings and helping children whenever she could. She never attended college and once believed she had failed in life because of it. But decades after she began working at the Aubrey Independent School District, the 76-year-old has received an honour she never imagined. According to WFAA-TV, on October 21, officials announced that a new elementary school would be named after her, recognising the years she spent caring for students and supporting the school community.Hampton's journey was not one she had always felt proud of. She grew up in a family of eight children and was the only one among her siblings to complete high school. However, she did not go on to college, something that troubled her for years. She later came to see her life differently, particularly after spending much of it working with children.Her job at the school district involved keeping classrooms and other facilities clean, but Hampton did not limit herself to those responsibilities. She helped children with their assignments, bought school supplies for students who needed them and sometimes gave them rides. She also worked at ticket booths during school football games. These were not part of her regular cleaning duties, but they became part of how she contributed to the district.Hampton retired from her custodial position in 2022 after 39 years of service. By then, she had become a familiar figure to students, teachers and staff members. Her years at the district eventually led officials to make the unusual decision of naming the new elementary school being built in Aubrey after her.When Hampton learn about the honourThe school district did not tell Hampton beforehand that it had decided to name the building after her. Instead, officials invited her to a meeting of the district's board of trustees on October 21. According to The Guardian, she had been asked to attend under the impression that she would be discussing a school-related matter.During the meeting, superintendent Shannon Saylor asked Hampton to unroll a red carpet near the speaker's podium. It was a familiar request for someone who had spent years helping prepare school facilities for different activities.Hampton went ahead with the task. But when she opened the carpet, she found a message she had not expected. Printed across it were the words “Marilyn Hampton Elementary School.”She immediately became emotional as people in the room applauded. Covering her face with her hands, Hampton struggled to respond. “You are too good. I wasn’t expecting this. Thank you all. I can’t speak,” she said, according to the New York Post.Board members came forward to hug her, while officials showed her an image of the new school with her name on the building.Hampton then realised she had not brought her phone to record the moment. Saylor joked that she did not need to worry because the announcement would be shared widely.Hampton's extraordinary contributionsThe district's decision reflected the role Hampton had played in children's lives during her years of service. Although her official job was to maintain school buildings, she often spent time helping students in other ways. Some needed assistance with schoolwork, while others required basic classroom supplies. Hampton helped wherever she could.Her involvement extended to school events as well. She worked at football games and remained connected with the wider school community.Saylor said Hampton had made an important contribution to students despite not holding a teaching position. “She may not have the official title of an educator, but she was in every meaningful sense a teacher and an educator at heart,” the superintendent said.According to The Guardian, thousands of students, teachers and staff members had been influenced by Hampton's commitment during her years at the district.The recognition also meant a great deal to Hampton personally because of her earlier doubts about not attending college.Speaking about how her thinking had changed, she said, “I just thought, ‘You know, Marilyn? God put you where you are supposed to be.’ And I am very happy with the way things turned out.”What is Marilyn Hampton doing now?Although Hampton retired from her custodial job in 2022, she has continued spending time with children. According to the New York Post, she now visits the district's Early Bird Learning Centre, where she has been seen sitting in a rocking chair and feeding a young girl named Claire.Following the school board announcement, the district also presented her with a T-shirt bearing the name of the new elementary school.Hampton later told WFAA that she was still overwhelmed by the recognition. “I still can’t believe it. I haven’t stopped crying,” she said.The new building, previously known as Elementary School Number Five, is scheduled to open in August 2027.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A Beverly Park mansion where Prince lived as a renter in 2008 has been cut by $13.5 million after first hitting the market at $68 million earlier this year; the estate sits on two acres in a gated enclave that has attracted residents such as Sylvester Stallone and Mark Wahlberg
articles.summary: Not every home in Los Angeles has a famous name. But this one does.
articles.body: Not every home in Los Angeles has a famous name. But this one does. The sprawling estate at 77 Beverly Park Lane, where Prince once lived, is on the market for $54.5 million after a $13.5 million price cut, Mansion Global reported. The megamansion was initially listed for $68 million, according to The Real Deal.A home with a famous tenantThe house sits at 77 Beverly Park Lane on two flat acres inside a guard-gated community. The late singer, né Prince Rogers Nelson, reportedly lived in the property and recorded there between 2008 and 2009, according to the outlet. The property was owned by an entity linked to Vanna White’s ex-husband, developer George Santopietro. He built the mansion in 2010. However, the mansion was built in 2007, according to its listing on Zillow. Branden Williams and Rayni Williams of The Beverly Hills Estates have listed the property.Inside the megamansionThe megamansion sits on what the listing describes as “the most prolific property in Beverly Park”. It adds: “A dramatic arrival unfolds into interiors defined by soaring ceilings, refined architectural detail, expansive volumes, and millions spent on stones and finishes sourced from around the world. Walls of glass frame the surrounding landscape, filling the home with natural light and seamlessly connecting indoor living with the estate's outdoor spaces.”The mansion spans 27,000 sq ft and has nine bedrooms and 15 bathrooms. The house is built for grand-scale entertaining, with a multimillion-dollar private theatre and an extraordinary wine cellar. It also comes with a gym and parking for more than 50 cars. The grounds are just as striking. The landscaping was designed by the renowned landscape designer behind San Ysidro Ranch. “Resort-calibre grounds showcase manicured lawns, lush rose and vegetable gardens, and entertaining terraces with multiple fire pits, an outdoor kitchen, pizza oven, grills, and dining areas, creating a private oasis,” the listing says.Beverly Park has long attracted people who value wealth and privacy. Sylvester Stallone lived there, and Adele bought his former estate in 2020 for $58 million. Mark Wahlberg also owned a home in the enclave. Paris Hilton and her husband, Carter Reum, bought that property last year.The megamansion first hit the market in April for $68 million. That was a high figure even for this neighbourhood. Other sellers on the same street have learnt the same lesson. In 2022, Villa Firenze came down by about $41 million from an asking price of $120 million, while Wahlberg cut his own asking price from $87.5 million to $79.5 million that same year.Those cuts suggest buyers in this enclave are willing to pay top dollar, but only for a home that matches recent sales. However, the Prince connection adds historical significance to the listing. The recent discount might also attract more interest from potential buyers.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Consett group painting rocks and hiding them around country
articles.summary: A rock painting group which started during lockdown has now got thousands of members.
articles.body:
A craft group has hit 8,000 members six years after they began hiding painted pebbles around the world.

Stephanie Winter and her aunt Victoria Morris set up Consett Rocks in 2020 to help people stay creative during the coronavirus pandemic.

Since then, Winter has painted hundreds of stones and the group has amassed thousands of members on social media, all posting painted pebbles they have hidden or found.

Winter said she had been "amazed" to see how large the group had become and to know how many strangers they had made smile.

"We created the group to help people in and around the Consett area get creative and active again during lockdown," Winter said.

"Everyone who has found a rock and shared it on the group has always said its made them happy."

She said some people who found the painted rocks left them where they were, others took them home for their gardens and some hid them in different locations.

Winter once hid a Consett Rock in Iceland and remarkably it made its way back to the UK.

Leanne Harris and her family first started painting rocks after discovering a Consett Rock while on a day out.

She said some of their creations had popped back up in entirely different countries months after being placed.

"My husband hid a rock in Durham in July 2025 and it was not seen again until it turned up in October in Australia," Harris said.

"We hid a little crab rock in Bowlees Visitor Centre [in Teesdale] and it was found by a family having a holiday before the mum's maternity leave ended, and they took it home and put it in their baby's memory box."

Harris recommended people give pebble painting a go because all you needed was "a simple little rock and a bit of paint which ends up making someone's day".

articles.title: Jennifer Lopez became Grameen America’s ambassador in 2022; the nonprofit now reports $8 billion in cumulative loans and 291,602 small businesses served as it expands access to business capital
articles.summary: For women starting businesses on a shoestring budget, access to capital can mean the difference between an idea staying a dream or becoming a living.
articles.body: For women starting businesses on a shoestring budget, access to capital can mean the difference between an idea staying a dream or becoming a living. Grameen America's model has been centered on bridging this gap, particularly for women who live in communities that require more assistance. The partnership with Jennifer Lopez brought a star-studded voice to that mission, driving more awareness around financial inclusion and Latina entrepreneurship.A partnership for Latina businesswomenLopez became Grameen America's National Ambassador in 2022 as part of her philanthropy, the blog reports. The partnership was created to assist Latina business owners who have historically been left out of mainstream financial services. Grameen America provides business capital, financial education, credit and asset building, and peer networks to women living below the federal poverty line. As an ambassador, Lopez would mentor Latina entrepreneurs, promote financial literacy and encourage pathways toward greater financial independence. The collaboration also aided Grameen America’s larger mission of reaching more Latina entrepreneurs throughout the United States.Access to building companiesThe organisation’s approach is more than just lending. Members receive ongoing financial literacy training and have their loan payments reported to credit bureaus. This enables members to establish their financial identities and gain access to improved financial services in the future. The Grameen America Blog has written about the extent of the problem for women entrepreneurs. Latino-owned businesses have grown quickly, but access to traditional lending has been uneven. Women also receive a tiny fraction of small business loans from mainstream financial institutions.Grameen America’s model seeks to address these gaps by providing a combination of affordable capital, education, savings and community-based support.Expanding national presenceThe organization has grown tremendously since then. Grameen America has provided more than $5 billion in affordable capital to more than 230,000 entrepreneurs in 29 U.S. cities, according to its website. “Reported figures to date indicate cumulative lending of around $8 billion, reaching 291,602 small businesses. And its aspirations for long-term growth are even bigger. The organization’s mission is to reach 750,000 entrepreneurs over the next 10 years and deploy $40 billion in loan capital to underserved communities.Invest in economic mobilityAccording to Grameen America’s website, the nonprofit will launch a five-year campaign supported by $600 million in new fundraising that combines philanthropy and debt capital. The initiative, combined with internally generated funding, is expected to help fund an estimated $1 billion investment to expand its program.The end goal is to help entrepreneurs move from financial stability to long-term economic mobility. Grameen America is dedicated to empowering neighborhood economies by assisting families in building generational wealth and financial independence through small business ownership.The mission was given a celebrity profile by Lopez, but the organization’s growing lending network suggests a larger ambition: to offer women historically excluded from the mainstream financial world the chance to own a business and access financial opportunity.Images Courtesy: istock and Instagram/jloYou use AI every day. articles.title: The power of dissent: How protests put leaders to the test in Brazil and Serbia
articles.summary: When students take to the streets, they are often dismissed as inexperienced, idealistic or easily mobilised.
articles.body: When students take to the streets, they are often dismissed as inexperienced, idealistic or easily mobilised. But when demonstrations persist, attract people beyond university campuses and begin challenging those in power, they can become a force that political leaders cannot ignore.The recent elections in Brazil and Serbia offer two different examples of how public dissent can reshape a political contest. In Brazil, student and youth mobilisation helped President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva recover from a first-round setback and defeat Flávio Bolsonaro in the presidential runoff. In Serbia, a student-led movement that began with demands for accountability following a deadly infrastructure disaster developed into an electoral challenge to the ruling establishment.Both outcomes can be described as victories for dissent, at least for now. But they also raise a harder question: can movements that mobilise people against those in power sustain their influence after the votes have been counted?Sudhir Kumar Suthar, a professor in political science at Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU), sees the results as part of a wider crisis of confidence in established political actors. “In the case of Brazil and Serbia, we can call the election results a victory of dissent, at least for the time being,” he said.Serbia: When a demand for answers became a challenge to powerSerbia’s student movement emerged after a concrete canopy collapsed at the railway station in Novi Sad in November 2024, killing 16 people. The tragedy triggered demands for accountability, transparency and the release of documents related to the disaster. As protests continued, anger over the incident became intertwined with broader concerns about corruption and the functioning of public institutions.Students blocked university faculties, organised demonstrations and marches, and attracted support beyond campuses. The movement increasingly challenged the government of President Aleksandar Vučić, whose Serbian Progressive Party had dominated the country's politics for years.The protests also drew on grievances that predated the Novi Sad disaster. Environmental concerns, particularly opposition to lithium mining, had already brought people onto the streets over fears about pollution, water resources and the consequences of industrial development. The disaster provided a new focal point for dissatisfaction that extended beyond a single incident.The movement’s decentralised structure became one of its defining features. Rather than depending on a single political leader, students organised through assemblies and collective decision-making. Their demands expanded from accountability for the disaster to early elections and broader institutional reform.The transition from protest to electoral politics was significant. A movement that began by demanding answers from the authorities was now challenging the established political order through the ballot box.In the recent snap parliamentary election, the student-backed Student List emerged ahead of the alliance led by Vučić. Preliminary results announced by Serbia’s Republic Electoral Commission on October 26 gave the Student List 52.71% of the votes counted and 140 seats in the 250-member parliament. The Vučić-led United Serbia list received 39.17% and 104 seats. These figures were preliminary, based on 8,187 of 8,392 polling stations processed at the time.The result marked a dramatic electoral setback for the ruling establishment and showed how a movement operating outside conventional party structures could turn public mobilisation into electoral strength.But an electoral victory does not automatically deliver institutional change. A movement united by opposition to corruption must now demonstrate that it can build consensus, govern effectively and implement its promises.“The student unrest shows distrust in political parties,” explained Suthar, adding that the question of what these movements ultimately want to replace the prevailing system with remains unresolved. “So basically it is a fight against the prevailing system without even thinking what it can be replaced with.”For Serbia’s student movement, the next test is whether it can turn its demands for accountability into transparent institutions and meaningful reforms.Brazil: Students mobilise against a political comebackBrazil’s election presented a different challenge. Rather than creating a new electoral force, students and youth movements mobilised against the prospect of a return of the Bolsonaro political camp.In the first round on October 4, Flávio Bolsonaro finished ahead of Lula, securing 47.03% of valid votes against the incumbent’s 45.16%. The result set up a closely contested runoff and energised supporters who feared that another Bolsonaro presidency would reverse policies on public services, minority rights and environmental protection.For Julia Andrade Maia, leader of the Juntos! movement and a student of the Federal University of Paraná, in Brazil, the mobilisation was driven by the experience of Jair Bolsonaro’s presidency from 2018 to 2022 and fears about what his son’s election could mean.“We have all learned something from what was the previous Bolsonaro government, and we definitely did not want to live through all that again,” said Julia.Julia described the prospect of another Bolsonaro presidency as a threat to public education, healthcare and democratic institutions. She said students were concerned about cuts to public resources amidst legacy of a government that she claimed attacked minorities and weakened public services.But the protests were not simply an endorsement of Lula. As Julia puts it, “I don't think people went to the streets because they thought Lula was perfect. People went to the streets because they knew Bolsonaro was terrible, and Lula was the only alternative that we had to face and defeat fascism.”Her account captures an important distinction between voting for a candidate and mobilising against a political alternative. The demonstrations brought together people who might not agree on every aspect of Lula’s agenda but shared concerns about the prospect of another Bolsonaro administration.How the streets amplified the campaignThe mobilisation began with students and youth movements, including student unions at universities across Brazil. Julia said that an early demonstration in Niterói, in Rio de Janeiro state, drew around 2,000 people. Within days, other universities were organising much larger protests.Political parties and other social movements subsequently joined the demonstrations. For Julia, the growth of the movement was inseparable from the relationship between physical gatherings and social media campaigning. “The streets made the digital stronger, as well as the digital engagements made the streets stronger,” she said.Julia said that seeing large crowds helped participants realise they were not alone, while social media enabled organisers to distribute content and extend their reach beyond the streets. Activists developed informal networks to circulate material on Instagram and other platforms, responding to what they perceived as unequal visibility for Lula’s campaign online.The demonstrations and digital mobilisation coincided with a campaign that gained momentum in the runoff. Lula ultimately won 51.79% of valid votes, receiving 64.26 million ballots against Flávio Bolsonaro’s 48.21%, or 59.83 million votes. He became the first Brazilian presidential candidate in the democratic era to finish second in the first round and then win the runoff.The environment, public services and sovereigntyThe Brazilian mobilisation was also about issues extending beyond the immediate contest between two candidates. Environmental protection, the Amazon rainforest, Indigenous rights and the management of natural resources were among the concerns shaping the political debate.Julia said that the environment was an important part of the mobilisation, though not its principal driver. “I think the environment played its role behind the protests, but I wouldn't say it was the major reason that the protests got so massive," she said.Environmental protection was not necessarily the single issue that brought the largest numbers onto the streets. Instead, it formed part of a wider set of concerns about public resources, national sovereignty, economic priorities and the role of the state.Suthar also cautioned against viewing the election as a straightforward environmental verdict. "In the case of Brazil, things are a bit complicated. The regions impacted by climate change are also the support base of Lula. Whereas the Bolsonaro support base is more in favour of industrialisation and modernisation, which is also being presented as the American model of governance.For environmental activists, Lula’s victory offers an opportunity to push for stronger forest protection and environmental enforcement. But it does not guarantee that those demands will be met. The government will still have to balance conservation with economic interests and navigate a legislature in which opposition forces remain influential.Can dissent produce lasting change?The similarities between Brazil and Serbia extend beyond the presence of students on the streets. In both countries, mobilisation connected immediate grievances with larger questions about how power is exercised and whose interests governments serve.Yet the movements also demonstrate that social media has not made physical protest redundant.“Social media is just an instrument to connect people more widely,” Suthar said. “But I don't think it has replaced the street-level protest as the medium of articulation of demands.”He argued that recent youth movements have revived a form of political participation that appeared to be receding. They have also brought together people who do not necessarily share a party membership or a single ideology but can unite around a common demand.The question is whether this solidarity survives after an election. Movements can lose momentum when the immediate target of their anger changes, while established political actors may absorb their demands without changing the structures that produced the original grievances.For Julia, Lula’s victory is not a reason for students to retreat from politics. She argues that Lula must learn from the mobilisation and continue working with citizens rather than assuming that an electoral mandate alone is sufficient.In Serbia, too, the student movement faces the challenge of converting electoral strength into accountable governance.The lesson from both countries is that sustained mobilisation can change the political stakes, challenge established power and create new possibilities for public accountability.The real measure of success, however, will come later — when protesters return to their campuses and communities, and the governments they helped shape demonstrate whether they have listened.You use AI every day. articles.title: Thieves steal around 100 brass memorial plaques from two South Australian cemeteries, including a tribute to a World War I veteran
articles.summary: Thieves have stolen around 100 brass memorial plaques from two cemeteries in South Australia, leaving families distressed and graves damaged.
articles.body: Thieves have stolen around 100 brass memorial plaques from two cemeteries in South Australia, leaving families distressed and graves damaged. The thefts were reported at Quorn and Wilmington, two communities in the state's north, about 40 kilometres apart. More than 80 plaques were taken from Quorn Cemetery, while 14 graves at Wilmington were also targeted.One of the stolen plaques honoured a World War I veteran. The thefts came to light in early March, prompting police to launch an investigation. According to ABC News, police have urged the public to come forward with information, and the state government has said it will work with the Flinders Ranges Council to fund replacements.Brass plaques removed from graves and memorials at QuornThe theft at Quorn cemetery was discovered on Friday morning, according to Flinders Ranges Council mayor Ken Anderson. More than 80 brass plaques were estimated to have been taken from the site. Most were removed from a rose garden where ashes were kept.Anderson said at least one of the affected memorials was less than six months old. He described the small community as being in total disbelief after the discovery.He said, "The thieves have either come along with a hammer and a chisel or a battery-operated set-up and they've prised these off and smashed some of the plinths that they were on."How did families discover the missing memorial plaquesThe second cemetery affected was at Wilmington, about 40 kilometres from Quorn. Keryn Corr visited the site with her husband Ross to see his parents’ graves and found that the brass plaque had been removed from their tombstone. She estimated that about 14 other graves had also been affected. Roslyn Roocke later checked the graves of her family members and discovered that the plaque for her great-uncle was missing.He had served in World War I. Roocke said the loss was upsetting and hurtful, and said the thieves had shown disrespect for those who fought in the wars and risked their lives.How have the thefts affected families and local communitiesThe mayors of the two council areas suspect the plaques were stolen to be sold for their material value. Anderson said brass contains copper and zinc, and believed the thefts were financially motivated. He urged anyone who was offered the plaques to report the matter. The mayor of the District Council of Mount Remarkable, Stephen McCarthy, said plaques had been taken from 14 graves at Wilmington. He said, "These people have had their identities stolen as well, so it really is a sad day for those people that are associated - the descendants, the townspeople”"These people might think they are very clever but they will get caught at some stage and we expect the law at its fullest could be executed onto these people."McCarthy said newer plaques made with a less expensive alloy were not taken, and that the thieves ‘know what they’re doing’.Police urge public to share information about stolen plaquesSouth Australia Police said officers were aware of the thefts and vandalism at both cemeteries. The force confirmed that an investigation was underway and urged anyone with information to contact police through Crime Stoppers.The theft at Quorn was discovered on Friday morning, while the damage at Wilmington came to light afterwards. On Sunday, the South Australian government said it would work with Flinders Ranges Council to fund the replacement of the memorials.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Noise complaint sees Kent rescue cockerel returned
articles.summary: Laura-Jane Wain says was threatened with a £1,500 fine over Bruce Almighty's crowing.
articles.body:
A woman said she has returned her rescue cockerel to an animal charity after she was issued an anti-social behaviour notice and threatened with a £1,500 fine following complaints over his early morning crowing.

Laura-Jane Wain, from Upper Halling, Kent, took in Bruce Almighty in 2025 and said she had not received a complaint until July, when the council first warned her to take steps to minimise the noise.

"It's not a constant sound, it was only every so often, and I loved it," she said. "I thought it was a gentle crowing."

Medway Council said it had a "statutory responsibility to investigate complaints that may be considered excessive, regular or constant - and that unreasonably interfere with the wellbeing, comfort or enjoyment of a resident's property".

Wain told the Local Democracy Reporting Service : "They [neighbours] never came to us to say, 'can you do something about it?'.

"They did not even put a letter through saying it was getting on their nerves or whatever. Nothing. Nobody ever commented on it.

"I have had supportive messages from people saying they like hearing the cockerel, that it feels like the country.

"It's a semi-rural area and the houses are quite far apart with a decent amount of land between them."

Following the first complaint, she said the council wrote to her with suggestions about possible ways to remedy the situation, including placing Bruce in a darkened space to make him think it was still night-time.

Wain said she followed the advice and took the cockerel into her home's cellar in the evening, bringing him out again later in the morning.

"That seemed to take the sting [out] but then we still got the second complaint," she said.

After receiving the second letter from Medway Council with the anti-social behaviour notice in September, Wain said she decided to return the cockerel.

"It's just quite sad that so many people did say to me they enjoyed hearing the cockerel," she said.

A spokesperson for the local authority added: "The evidence collected by the council included diary sheets from residents, which logged dates, times and how they were being affected by a noise disturbance, which was then following by an investigation by officers."

articles.title: 'Stop climbing up trees': Israeli president urges parties to avert fresh election
articles.summary: Israeli President Isaac Herzog has urged political parties to accept the election outcome and work towards forming a government, warning that another
articles.body: Israeli President Isaac Herzog has urged political parties to accept the election outcome and work towards forming a government, warning that another election should be avoided. His appeal comes as neither the opposition nor the ruling coalition has secured a clear majority in the 120-member Knesset, Israel's parliament.Speaking at a memorial ceremony for Israel's first president, Chaim Weizmann, Herzog asked party leaders to acknowledge the results and find a way forward.“Stop climbing up trees and face the reality”, he said, urging political leaders to move beyond their election campaign positions and negotiate.According to The Times of Israel, Herzog said he would receive the official results from Central Elections Committee chairman Justice Noam Solberg on Wednesday, November 4.“This coming Wednesday, I will receive the official election results from the Central Elections Committee chairman… Justice Noam Solberg.”He said consultations with political parties would begin afterwards at the President's Residence, which would be open to all factions.“The President’s Residence will be wide open to all factions and parties,” he added.Herzog urges parties to avoid another electionHerzog called on political leaders to look for ways to form a government rather than take the country through another election campaign.“As we all know, during an election campaign, naturally and predictably, candidates climb high up into the trees,” he said.“But the elections are over, the election results are an established fact — they are reality. And this is the time to tell all the leaders: stop climbing the trees and face reality. This week at the President’s Residence, we will try to put up ladders, to enable the leaders to face reality, in a measured and careful manner,” he said.The final certified results are due to be submitted to Herzog on November 4, after checks for possible discrepancies. The newly elected Knesset is scheduled to take oath on November 10.Opposition faces challenge despite seat advantageThe opposition secured 67 seats in Tuesday's election, compared with 53 for the coalition led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. However, the opposition's numbers are divided between 48 seats held by Zionist parties and 19 won by Arab non-Zionist parties, making it difficult to agree on a governing arrangement.On Saturday, Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the opposition Yashar party, said he would move quickly to use the new Knesset's parliamentary majority. He argued that voters had delivered a clear verdict against Netanyahu's government.Eisenkot said he wanted to form a broad "Zionist and statesmanlike government" and that any lawmaker willing to support his basic conditions could become a partner. He also called for a major effort to prevent another election and a prolonged political deadlock.Arab parties' support and alternative proposalsThe Arab non-Zionist parties, Joint List and Ra'am, are reportedly expected to recommend Eisenkot for prime minister during their consultations with Herzog. The Jerusalem Post reported this, citing a senior Joint List official who spoke to Israeli outlet Walla.Meanwhile, opposition parties are said to be considering legislation that would introduce direct elections for prime minister. According to The Times of Israel, the proposal could offer a way to form a minority government without relying on the support of Arab parties.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Another 'exploding pager' plot? Israel eyes strike on Tehran’s top military bosses
articles.summary: Israel is considering a covert operation modelled on its 2024 exploding-pager attacks against Hezbollah to target Iran's top military and security
articles.body: Israel is considering a covert operation modelled on its 2024 exploding-pager attacks against Hezbollah to target Iran's top military and security leadership, potentially eliminating key commanders and disrupting the country's wartime command structure, amid growing uncertainty over the possibility of renewed US-Israeli strikes against Tehran."According to a report published by the New York Post, former Mossad deputy head of global operations Oded Ailam said Israel could consider a pager-style operation targeting Iran's military establishment, describing the option as 'fully on the table'."He identified four senior figures as the people exercising real power in Tehran, including Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) chief Ahmad Vahidi, Basij commander Hossein Taeb, armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi and security official Mohsen Rezaei.Ailam argued that Iran's military establishment has emerged as the principal centre of power, with the country's political leadership struggling to maintain control over strategic decisions. He suggested that disagreements between military hardliners and political officials have also complicated Tehran's negotiations with Washington.The proposed operation draws parallels with Israel's September 2024 covert campaign against Hezbollah, widely referred to as Operation Grim Beeper, in which thousands of pagers and walkie-talkies used by the Iran-backed militant group exploded across Lebanon in two successive waves.The first wave began on September 17, 2024, when thousands of pagers used by Hezbollah operatives exploded almost simultaneously across Lebanon, particularly in Beirut's southern suburbs, the Bekaa Valley and southern Lebanon. The following day, September 18, a second wave targeted handheld walkie-talkies used by the group, triggering explosions in several locations, including during funerals. The two attacks killed at least 39 people and injured more than 3,400, according to Reuters.According to Reuters, Hezbollah had ordered approximately 5,000 AR-924 pagers, which were allegedly modified before reaching the group. Explosives were concealed inside the devices, allowing Israeli intelligence to turn ordinary communication equipment into remotely activated weapons.In December 2024, two former Israeli intelligence officers, speaking anonymously to CBS News' 60 Minutes, disclosed further details about the operation. They said the planning had begun nearly a decade earlier with booby-trapped walkie-talkies, while the pager component was developed from 2022 onwards.The report comes amid growing indications that Washington and Tel Aviv are preparing for a possible resumption of military operations against Iran after the November 3 US midterm elections. A third American aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, is heading towards the Middle East, where it is expected to join the USS George Washington and USS George HW Bush, already deployed in the region.US President Donald Trump told Kansas City radio station KCMO on Friday that the war was "going to get wrapped up soon", without providing details about how or when the conflict would end, according to the report.Retired US Army General Jack Keane argued that any renewed American and Israeli military campaign should target Iran's military leadership alongside its nuclear programme, domestic energy infrastructure and ballistic missile and drone facilities.You use AI every day. articles.title: Executive action & emergencies: How Trump plans to deal with Democrat-controlled Congress after US midterms
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump's administration is preparing for the possibility of Democrats taking control of Congress after Tuesday's midterm elections,
articles.body: US President Donald Trump's administration is preparing for the possibility of Democrats taking control of Congress after Tuesday's midterm elections, drawing up plans to continue advancing his agenda through executive powers while bracing for investigations into his government.Senior aides, including deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and budget director Russell Vought, have been working with the White House Counsel's Office since April to identify measures Trump could pursue without congressional approval, reported news agency Reuters.These include policies on immigration, tariffs, housing costs and federal spending, according to a White House official and two people familiar with the plans.White House lawyers are also examining what Trump can legally do independently, how far he can push his authority and how to defend those decisions in court.White House plans for a Democratic CongressDemocrats need to gain four seats in both the House of Representatives and the Senate to take control. Polls favour them in the House, while the Senate contest remains too close to call.A Democratic majority would allow the party to block legislation, scrutinise government spending and investigate the administration. However, Trump would retain considerable executive authority over trade, foreign policy and federal agencies.Trump has spent the past month campaigning to help Republicans retain control of Congress, even as his aides prepare for a possible shift in power in 2027.The White House dismissed suggestions of Republican losses, accusing the media of promoting a false narrative."This administration and commonsense Republicans will continue to secure our borders, restore law and order, putting more money back into the pockets of hard-working Americans, and deliver wins for the American people," spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.Measures under consideration include fresh tariffs on critical minerals and wind turbines, tighter visa rules for international students and temporary foreign workers, and steps to reduce housing and construction costs.Vought is examining how the administration could use funds already approved by Congress to pursue Trump's priorities. He is also considering changes to federal grant rules that would give political appointees greater influence over how government funds are allocated.Trump has been briefed on the plans and taken part in discussions. Asked how comfortable Trump would be governing through executive powers under a Democratic Congress, one person familiar with the preparations said, "very comfortable."Executive powers have limitsSince returning to office in January 2025, Trump has used executive authority to impose tariffs, intensify immigration enforcement, reduce the federal workforce and pursue foreign policy objectives, including the war against Iran, without fresh congressional approval."President Trump in the last two years has basically ignored Congress and tried to do as much as possible through executive orders and executive power," said Nathan Gonzales, editor at Inside Elections. "I think he will only continue if there are Democratic majorities."A Democratic-controlled Senate could block Trump's judicial and senior administration nominees, while both chambers could refuse to pass legislation he supports. Courts could also strike down executive actions that exceed his legal authority.Trump braces for congressional probeOne challenge the US president cannot avoid through executive action is congressional scrutiny. House Democrats and committee staff have discussed using hearings, subpoenas and document requests to investigate whether Trump has used his office to benefit himself, allies or donors, Reuters previously reported.White House lawyers have been briefing political appointees and agency heads on how to respond to congressional inquiries and have advised officials to be careful about what they put in writing.The administration has also sought a Justice Department opinion that could allow Trump to invoke executive privilege to shield communications with private advisers from congressional scrutiny, one person familiar with the matter said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Yash's seven-year-old son watched his father play Ravana in Ramayana and cried during the Jatayu scene, saying he should not have killed the bird even in a film; the actor says he had to explain the role
articles.summary: Yash may be playing Ravana in Nitesh Tiwari’s ‘Ramayana,’ but his seven-year-old son Yatharv was not prepared to see his father kill someone (Jatayu) on
articles.body: Yash may be playing Ravana in Nitesh Tiwari’s ‘Ramayana,’ but his seven-year-old son Yatharv was not prepared to see his father kill someone (Jatayu) on screen. During the film’s world premiere in Los Angeles, the young boy became emotional while watching the scene in which Ravana attacks Jatayu, the vulture who tries to stop him from abducting Sita. He later told his father that he did not like what he had done, even though it was only a film.Yash and his co-star Sai Pallavi, who plays Sita, recalled the incident during a recent media interaction. Yash had attended the premiere at the Academy Museum in Los Angeles on October 27 with his children, Ayra and Yatharv. It was the first time either child had watched a film in a theatre. Speaking about their reaction, Yash said, “I could see they had so many questions because for them, life is just starting. They are understanding how to behave, how to respect one another. I was so surprised to see my son’s reaction.”Sai Pallavi then shared what had upset Yatharv. “He said to Yash, ‘I didn’t like you killing that bird,’” she recalled. She explained that the child knew his father was an actor and had appeared in films before. He also understood that the events on screen were part of a performance. But that did not stop him from feeling upset.“He knows that it is his daddy and that he has done movies before and that maybe they were acting. But he said, ‘No, it is not nice. It is not good that you kill the bird even in the movie. I don’t think you should have done that.’ It was such a beautiful moment,” Sai Pallavi said.The scene appears to have left a stronger impression on the child than the distinction between his father's real life and the character he was playing. For Yatharv, Ravana killing Jatayu was still something his father should not have done.Why Yash wanted to portray Ravana differentlyYash also spoke about the challenge of playing Ravana, a character whose strength and power are central to the story. He said his biggest challenge was making audiences believe that Ravana was almost impossible to defeat. “For me, to make everybody believe that it is impossible to defeat him, that he is invincible, getting to that phase was the challenging part,” he said.The actor explained that simply having a powerful character on screen was not enough. He had to make the audience believe in that power through his performance. “When you are portraying that role, if you are not convinced yourself and if you are not presenting it in the manner it is supposed to be, people will not feel it. I may fail the whole thing where people say, ‘He is good, but the role is good.’ There is a difference between Ravana being strong and me portraying Ravana to be strong. That is the gap I am talking about,” he added.Yash also wanted to move beyond the familiar portrayal of Ravana as a character who is simply evil. He said he was interested in showing audiences another side of the mythological figure and allowing them to understand his motivations and mistakes.“Sometimes you want to give people another point of view, give them an opportunity to understand that he also had some good qualities. It is not just black and white. To let people reason with him, understand what he was trying to do and where he went wrong. That was quite interesting and challenging for me,” he said.For Yash, the premiere offered an opportunity to see his children watch him in one of his most significant roles. But while audiences may be looking forward to seeing his interpretation of Ravana, his son’s response to the Jatayu scene showed that, at least for one young viewer, the character's actions mattered more than the fact that his father was only acting.Directed by Nitesh Tiwari, ‘Ramayana’ stars Ranbir Kapoor as Ram, Sai Pallavi as Sita, Yash as Ravana, Sunny Deol as Hanuman and Ravi Dubey as Lakshman. The film is scheduled for a worldwide theatrical release on November 5, 2026.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ testGet the latest Lifestyle News and more. articles.title: No paneer, no honey, no milky chai? The real challenge of going vegan in India
articles.summary: For many Indians, the day begins with a cup of milky chai, followed by breakfast cooked in ghee.
articles.body: For many Indians, the day begins with a cup of milky chai, followed by breakfast cooked in ghee. Lunch may come with a bowl of curd and paneer on the menu, while a Sunday meal is often incomplete without chicken curry.These familiar food habits are so deeply woven into everyday life that giving up all animal-derived products can seem like a difficult choice.But for people who turn vegan, the change goes beyond replacing meat with vegetables. It means rethinking everyday ingredients, from milk and butter to honey, as well as choices involving clothing, cosmetics and other products.“There are alternatives for practically everything. You can make curd at home using plant milk, use tofu instead of paneer, and use different nut and soy milks,” says Sarahana, who has been vegan since 2018.On World Vegan Day, observed on November 1, the question is not just why people choose veganism, but what it takes to follow the lifestyle.What is veganism?According to The Vegan Society, veganism is a way of living that seeks to exclude, as far as possible and practicable, all forms of animal exploitation and cruelty.While a vegan diet avoids meat, fish, eggs, dairy and honey, the lifestyle also extends to products made from animals, those tested on animals and activities that use animals for entertainment.For some, the decision is rooted in animal welfare; for others, environmental concerns or health considerations play a role.But the experiences of vegans show that the transition is as much about changing everyday habits as it is about changing one's perspective.India has a long tradition of vegetarian food, but veganism goes a step further by excluding all animal-derived products, including milk, curd, ghee, paneer and honey.According to estimates compiled by World Population Review, around 9% of India's population followed a vegan diet in 2021, amounting to an estimated 121.5 million people. The country also has a substantial vegetarian population, reflecting its diverse food traditions.However, the figure should be treated as an estimate rather than a definitive count, as veganism surveys often rely on self-reported responses and vary in methodologies.What does a vegan Indian kitchen look like?A vegan diet does not necessarily mean giving up familiar Indian food or relying on expensive, imported alternatives. Dal, rice, roti, rajma, chole, idli, dosa, poha, upma and vegetable dishes can all be part of a vegan diet, provided they are prepared without animal-derived ingredients.Utkarsh Garg, a representative of People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA), says their meals are a mix of familiar Indian dishes and plant-based alternatives.“Breakfast is usually a protein smoothie bowl or soaked oats, although I’m definitely not above a plate of poha, chhole-kulche or one enormous aloo paratha when the mood strikes!”“Lunch and dinner usually include things like tofu, soybeans, dals, rajma and plenty of vegetables. My current obsession is tempeh. I seem to be finding increasingly creative excuses to put it into everything I eat.”“As for living without milk, paneer, curd or ghee, I genuinely don’t find it difficult anymore. There are so many vegan alternatives available now, and many things are surprisingly easy and inexpensive to make at home as well.” Utkarsh said.Sarahana says she relies largely on everyday Indian food rather than packaged substitutes.“As for food, my everyday diet is actually quite simple and Indian. Dal, rice, roti, vegetables, chickpeas, rajma, seasonal produce and different legumes. There are so many naturally plant-based foods available in India. You don’t need expensive imported alternatives or packaged vegan products to survive without dairy.“There are alternatives for practically everything. You can make curd at home using plant milk, use tofu instead of paneer, and use different nut and soy milks. Ghee is essentially clarified butter, and personally, I don’t feel the need to replace it.”The distinction is important. A vegan diet does not require a direct substitute for every non-vegan food. It can instead be built around naturally plant-based ingredients that are already widely used in Indian kitchens.Why are people choosing veganism?For Utkarsh, the decision began in childhood. Watching a chicken being slaughtered made them connect the food on their plate with the animal it came from. He turned vegetarian that day and later went vegan.“For me, veganism has always been about animals. I’ve loved animals for as long as I can remember. While most kids my age were watching Cartoon Network or Pogo, I was glued to National Geographic, completely fascinated by dogs, cats, cows, snakes, and pretty much every animal I came across,” Utkarsh said.As he learnt more about animal exploitation, vegetarianism no longer felt enough. “My love for animals naturally led me to veganism. I’ve been vegan for four years now, and honestly, it is one of the best decisions I have ever made. More than changing what I eat or wear, it has changed the way I look at the world and my place in it.”For Sarahana, the turning point came in 2018, when she watched a video of a pregnant cow being slaughtered after she was no longer productive for the dairy industry.“My decision came from questioning something very basic: why do we, as human beings, consider ourselves superior to other animals? Why do we love some animals, consider some family, see some as entertainment, and others as food?” she said.While studying gender, Sarahana began drawing parallels between the exploitation of women's bodies and that of female animals in the dairy industry.“How can I study feminism, gender and the exploitation of female bodies and not extend that understanding beyond human beings? How can I talk about patriarchy and exploitation while continuing to pay an industry that repeatedly impregnates female animals, takes away their babies and exploits their reproductive systems?” she said.Coming from a Dalit community, Sarahana also views veganism through the lens of social justice, questioning how societies decide whose lives are valued.“We love cats and dogs, welcome them into our homes and call them family, but we look at chickens, goats and buffaloes and see food. We have created categories of animals that deserve affection and animals that can be exploited,” she added.The price of going veganOne common perception is that veganism is an expensive lifestyle, largely because plant-based milk, meat substitutes and other packaged alternatives can cost more than conventional products. However, both Utkarsh and Sarahana say that a vegan diet need not depend on these products.Utkarsh points out that many Indian staples are naturally plant-based. “India is one of the easiest places in which to eat vegan, because so much of the food we already know and love either naturally contains no animal-derived ingredients or can be veganised with ridiculously small changes.“Think about dal, rajma, chole, idli, dosa, poha, upma, roti, sabzis, rice dishes and countless regional foods. Veganism doesn’t have to mean buying an expensive imported mock meat or drinking a fancy packaged plant milk every morning. Those products are great if you enjoy them, but they aren’t what veganism depends on.”Sarahana agrees that the bigger challenge is often social rather than financial.“I don’t think being vegan in India is inherently expensive. Our traditional food already has so many affordable plant-based options. What can become expensive is the packaged vegan alternatives, not the basic diet itself. The bigger challenge is social conditioning. At family gatherings, weddings or even casual conversations, you constantly have to explain why you don’t consume something that everyone else considers normal.”Both say their families initially had questions and reservations. Utkarsh says their family is now supportive and has started incorporating more vegan foods and products into their lives. Sarahana, meanwhile, says she continues to face comments that she has been “brainwashed”.Is a vegan diet actually healthier?Veganism is often associated with better health, but a plant-based diet is not automatically a balanced one. Its nutritional value depends on the foods included and whether essential nutrients are adequately supplied.Dt Gausiya Aziz, consultant and head of nutrition and dietetics at SPARSH Hospital, Yelahanka, says a well-planned vegan diet can support cardiovascular and metabolic health.“Research suggests that plant-based dietary patterns rich in fibre, antioxidants and unsaturated fats can help lower LDL cholesterol, improve blood pressure and support healthy weight management. They may also reduce the risk of developing type 2 diabetes,” she says.However, claims that veganism automatically prevents cancer, reverses chronic diseases or guarantees a longer life are exaggerated, she cautions. Health outcomes depend on overall diet quality, lifestyle and individual medical conditions.A key concern is meeting nutritional requirements. Vitamin B12, iron, calcium, vitamin D, iodine, zinc, omega-3 fatty acids and protein need particular attention.Vitamin B12 is especially important because reliable natural plant-based sources are limited. Fortified foods or supplements may therefore be necessary.Aziz recommends a varied diet containing whole grains, legumes, vegetables, fruits, nuts and seeds, along with appropriate supplementation and regular nutritional assessment.Utkarsh says he pay close attention to their nutritional needs and take vitamin B12 supplements.“I am also quite particular about my nutrition. I take my B12 regularly and pay attention to vitamin D and other essential nutrients. B12 supplementation is important for vegans, and these supplements are accessible at pharmacies,” he said.The PETA representative added that he has noticed less bloating since turning vegan and feel healthier, but stresses that dietary planning matters.“Of course, I think any diet needs to be properly planned rather than treated as automatically healthy simply because it carries a particular label. For me, veganism has actually made me more conscious of what I eat and what my body needs.”Aziz also warns that highly processed vegan foods are not necessarily healthy. Packaged snacks, meat substitutes and desserts can contain high amounts of sodium, refined carbohydrates, added sugars and saturated fats. She advises prioritising minimally processed foods and checking nutritional labels.“Children, pregnant women and older adults have specific nutritional requirements that demand careful consideration before adopting a vegan diet. During childhood, adequate energy, protein, calcium, iron, vitamin B12 and vitamin D are essential for growth and development. Pregnant women must additionally ensure sufficient folate, iodine, choline and omega-3 fatty acids to support maternal health and fetal development. Older adults should prioritise protein intake, calcium and vitamin D to preserve muscle strength and bone health. Vitamin B12 supplementation is particularly important across these groups,” Aziz added.Nutritionist Aziz also recommends consulting a qualified dietitian or healthcare professional before making significant dietary changes.Is veganism about health, animals or the planet?Animal welfare is not the only reason people choose veganism. Environmental concerns are also part of the conversation.Aziz says vegan diets generally have a lower environmental footprint than diets containing substantial amounts of animal products, particularly red meat and dairy.Plant-based food production typically requires less agricultural land and generates fewer greenhouse gas emissions than livestock farming. It can also reduce pressure on biodiversity and freshwater resources.However, the environmental impact varies with farming methods, transportation, processing and food waste. Choosing locally available, seasonal and minimally processed plant foods can help reduce the footprint further.For Utkarsh, the values behind veganism are also connected to ideas of compassion and non-violence.“We grow up hearing about ahimsa and vasudhaiva kutumbakam, the idea that the world is one family. To me, animals shouldn’t be excluded from that circle of compassion simply because they belong to another species,” he said.What should you know before going vegan?Going vegan involves more than changing what is on the plate. It can mean checking product labels, asking about ingredients when eating out and finding alternatives to everyday items.Some medications and personal-care products may also contain animal-derived ingredients, making it important to check rather than assume that a product is vegan.For someone considering the transition, Utkarsh suggests starting by understanding where everyday products come from.“For anyone considering going vegan because they care about animals, I would say: start by looking. Look honestly at where our milk, meat, eggs, leather, wool, silk, cosmetics and entertainment come from.”“Once I did that, veganism stopped feeling like something I was ‘giving up’. It started feeling like the most natural extension of something I had believed all along.”Sarahana says the idea is to extend compassion beyond the animals people traditionally consider companions or pets.She also points to the growing number of Indian businesses offering vegan alternatives. For her, such businesses are helping make animal-free choices more accessible.For those thinking of making the switch, the practical starting point may be simple: understand what a vegan diet excludes, plan for essential nutrients and explore the plant-based foods already available in the kitchen.World Vegan Day was established in 1994 by Louise Wallis, then president of The Vegan Society, to mark the 50th anniversary of the organisation's founding in November 1944.The day is now observed annually on November 1 to raise awareness about veganism and its ethical, environmental and health-related aspects.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Delhi AQI at 261, worst this season: New winter curbs begin with traffic snarls; know what restrictions are in force
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi's new winter pollution curbs triggered long traffic jams at the city's borders on Sunday, as vehicles lined up for emission checks on the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi's new winter pollution curbs triggered long traffic jams at the city's borders on Sunday, as vehicles lined up for emission checks on the first day of enforcement.The congestion came alongside a sharp deterioration in air quality, with the city's Air Quality Index (AQI) rising to 261 in the poor category — its worst reading of the season and the highest in 198 days.Heavy traffic was reported at several entry points, particularly along the Delhi-Gurugram and Delhi-Noida borders, where traffic police and enforcement teams checked vehicles entering the national capital.Long queues built up near Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) toll booths and other entry points across the National Capital Region (NCR).Commuters faced bumper-to-bumper traffic as officials stopped vehicles that failed to meet the prescribed emission standards.Delhi's AQI stood at 261 on Sunday, matching the reading recorded on July 12. The index had last crossed the 250 mark on April 17, when it stood at 263.Of the 57 air quality monitoring stations across the city, 22 recorded air quality in the very poor category, 21 reported poor air quality and the remaining 14 registered moderate levels.Jahangirpuri recorded the highest AQI at 378, close to the severe category, which begins at 401. PM2.5 remained the predominant pollutant in the national capital.The worsening air quality coincided with the rollout of a series of special winter pollution-control measures. These include restrictions on vehicles registered outside Delhi that conform to BS-IV or older emission standards, a ban on dust-generating outdoor construction activities, a doubling of parking charges and a cap of 50% on physical attendance in government and private offices.The restrictions will remain in force for different periods between November 1 and February 28. They are aimed at curbing vehicular emissions, dust pollution and traffic congestion during the winter months.Round-the-clock checks at bordersEnforcement teams have begun round-the-clock inspections to ensure compliance with the new measures. Automatic number plate recognition cameras installed at entry points and other key locations are being used to identify vehicles violating the restrictions.The Delhi transport department has deployed around 250 enforcement personnel at major entry points, toll plazas and identified pollution hotspots.A total of 39 teams have been stationed across 13 major toll plazas, including DND, Rajokri on NH-48, Ghazipur, Singhu border, Tikri and Badarpur.Officials have been instructed to act against vehicles that do not comply with the restrictions. Action includes issuing electronic challans and impounding vehicles in accordance with the rules.Commuters question effectiveness of pollution curbsThe congestion at Delhi's entry points also drew criticism on social media, with commuters complaining about long queues and questioning whether the restrictions would lead to a meaningful improvement in air quality."If you are travelling to Delhi in the next few days, you will have to bear the brunt of this type of traffic. Plan accordingly. Delhi-NCR's air quality will have zero improvement because of this step," a social media user posted.Another commuter said: "Three hours stuck at the Delhi border. What is the use of us even coming? The event I was supposed to attend was already halfway through. These restrictions are meant to reduce pollution, but commuters are being left stranded in endless traffic jams. And the funny thing is, it may not even prove effective in improving air quality."Construction ban, higher parking charges and work-from-home capThe restrictions also include a ban on all dust-generating demolition and outdoor civil construction activities from November 1 to January 31. Specified essential public infrastructure projects are exempt, subject to prescribed conditions.A complete ban on construction and demolition activities, barring specified exemptions, will also be in place from December 10 to January 20.Parking charges at authorised parking lots across Delhi have been doubled for the period from November 1 to February 28. Government and private offices have been asked to limit physical attendance to 50%, with the remaining employees working from home.Essential and emergency services have been exempted from the attendance restrictions.In a move aimed at easing traffic congestion, MCD offices will operate from 8.30 am to 5 pm, while state government offices will function from 10 am to 6.30 pm.Transport emissions account for 16.4% of contributionAccording to the Decision Support System (DSS) for air quality management, transport emissions accounted for 16.4% of Delhi's pollution contribution on articles.body: NAGPUR: Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis and Union minister Nitin Gadkari will lead a BJP march in Nagpur on November 5, marking the culmination of the party's nationwide 'Save Democracy, Remove Anarchy' campaign.The march, which is expected to draw between 15,000 and 20,000 participants, is part of the BJP's effort to counter what it has described as misleading propaganda by Opposition parties about democratic institutions.Senior BJP leader and state Revenue Minister Chandrashekhar Bawankule told reporters on Sunday that the march will begin at Yashwant Stadium and conclude at Samvidhan Chowk.As part of the 'Lokshahi Vachava-Arajakta Hatva' campaign, a series of programmes will be organised in Nagpur from November 2 to 5, he said.According to a party release, the events will focus on electoral integrity, the voting rights of eligible citizens and public confidence in democratic and constitutional institutions.The four-day programme will offer students, youth, social media influencers, intellectuals and members of the general public an opportunity to engage with issues related to democracy, Bawankule said.
